criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Introduction names three ethical issues—risk-based test coverage, treating data loss as harmless, and conflict of interest—and links them to design and organisational decision-making. Table 1 identifies stakeholders, interests and decisions, including patients with no decision power. This meets Excellent.

evidence.quote: Three ethical issues follow. First, test coverage is being set by the release calendar instead of by risk
Table 1 summarises who they are, what each has at stake and what each can decide.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: It gives substantive for-and-against arguments, then tests them against the health contract. Options table and recommendations draw conclusions for Rachel, management, health department, supplier and engineers. Balanced and stakeholder-specific, so Excellent.

evidence.quote: Shipping on time protects a real competitive advantage.
The strongest objection is harm to people who have no say.
Options B and C respect every stakeholder's interests better than either extreme.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: The report moves logically from issues to arguments, decision rule, options and conclusion. The conclusion follows from the evidence and rule, and stakeholder consequences are systematically covered. Compelling and well supported.

evidence.where: How should Rachel decide when to ship?
evidence.quote: Neither "never ship a defect" nor "ship unless someone could be physically hurt" is adequate.
The ethical course is to ship only when the risk has been measured, reduced where practical and accepted by an informed customer.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Eight reputable references support the argument, including four external cases, a code and a standard. Quantitative evidence (81 trusts, 19,000 appointments, US$475m, US$4.3bn) and qualitative reasoning are balanced. Excellent.

evidence.quote: at least 81 of 236 hospital trusts in England were disrupted, an estimated 19,000 appointments were cancelled
Intel had to offer replacements and took a charge of US$475 million
National Audit Office, "Investigation: WannaCry cyber attack and the NHS," HC 414

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: Abstract, introduction, discussion, conclusion, recommendations and references are present. Tables and a clear flowchart support the discussion. Prose is fluent and concise; IEEE-style references are consistent. Excellent.

evidence.quote: This report examines the dilemma of a quality assurance engineer, Rachel
C. Bartlett, "To ship or not to ship," Markkula Center for Applied Ethics

requirements.where: How should Rachel decide when to ship?; The Most Ethical Path
Introduction; Table 1; Arguments for shipping; Arguments against shipping; Table 2

technical_issues.issue: WannaCry figure says 'at least 81 of 236 hospital trusts'; NAO reports 81 trusts affected, so 'at least' is imprecise but not material.
Claim that the revenue argument 'holds only if the defect never causes a costly failure' is overstated; expected-value risk acceptance could still justify revenue with disclosure and safeguards.

overall: All five criteria are Excellent (10/10). The report is well structured, balanced, evidence-rich and stakeholder-aware, with a clear decision rule and justified recommendations. Minor imprecision in the WannaCry figure and one overstated revenue claim do not materially weaken it.

feedback.summary: Your report is assessed as Excellent across all five criteria. You frame three ethical issues in the Introduction, use Table 1 to map stakeholders, and build a balanced case through the for/against arguments, decision rule, options and recommendations. Evidence from WannaCry, Intel and others is strong. Minor refinements: tighten the WannaCry 'at least 81' wording and qualify the revenue claim in Arguments for shipping.
next_steps: In Arguments against shipping, revise 'at least 81 of 236 hospital trusts' to match the NAO wording exactly (81 trusts affected) and avoid 'at least' unless you can source it.

In Arguments for shipping, qualify the claim that the revenue argument 'holds only if the defect never causes a costly failure'; acknowledge that expected-value risk acceptance with disclosure and safeguards could still justify revenue.

To consolidate the top band, add a short sensitivity check or decision matrix in 'How should Rachel decide when to ship?' showing how Options B and C change under different defect probabilities and severities, linked to Table 2.

criteria.C1: Your Introduction names three ethical issues—risk-based test coverage, treating data loss as harmless, and conflict of interest—and links them to design and organisational decision-making. Table 1 maps stakeholders, interests and decision power, including patients. This is Excellent. To secure the top band, keep the stakeholder table tightly tied to each issue and avoid letting context become descriptive rather than analytical.
criteria.C2: You give substantive for-and-against arguments in Arguments for shipping and Arguments against shipping, then test them against the health contract. The options table and The Most Ethical Path draw conclusions for Rachel, management, the health department, supplier and engineers. Excellent. To secure it, make the stakeholder-specific conclusions even more explicit for each group rather than clustering them.
criteria.C3: Your report moves logically from issues to arguments, decision rule, options and Conclusion. The conclusion follows from your evidence and rule, and stakeholder consequences are covered systematically. Excellent. To secure the top band, signpost the decision rule earlier and show in the options table how each option follows from it, so the argument chain is unmistakable.
criteria.C4: Eight reputable references, including four external cases, a code and a standard, support your argument. Quantitative evidence (81 trusts, 19,000 appointments, US$475m, US$4.3bn) and qualitative reasoning are balanced. Excellent. To secure it, correct the WannaCry 'at least 81' wording and qualify the revenue claim in Arguments for shipping so the evidence is precise.
criteria.C5: Abstract, Introduction, discussion, Conclusion, Recommendations and References are present. Tables and a clear flowchart support the discussion; prose is fluent and concise, and IEEE-style references are consistent. Excellent. To secure it, ensure every visual element is explicitly referenced and interpreted in the text, and keep table captions self-contained.
